newsitem.title: UK: IMRO says action on MGAM averted damage to London.
newsitem.headline: IMRO says action on MGAM averted damage to London.

text.p: Investments watchdog IMRO said on Wednesday that swift action in dealing with problems at two of Deutsche Bank's British fund management subsidiaries had saved the City of London suffering significant damage to its reputation.

"Effective negotiation of compensation and rapid and substantial discipline by IMRO has significantly limited damage to the reputation of the City as a leading financial centre," IMRO's Phillip Thorpe said.

Earlier the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation imposed a record two million pound ($3.3 million) fine on two Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) subsidiaries for a catalogue of rule breaches and management failings connected with what has become widely-known as the Peter Young affair.
Young was sacked by MGAM in September after the suspension of three funds due to the discovery of serious irregularities in the valuations of unlisted securities.
Young's activities are currently under investigation by the Serious Fraud Office. He denies any criminal activity.

"The management of Morgan Grenfell failed to control the operation of its business and ignored clear and repeated warnings with severe adverse financial results," Thorpe, IMRO's chief executive, said in a statement.
He said IMRO had imposed the largest fine ever to be levied under Britain's 1986 Financial Services Act and had also secured the largest compensation package for investors.

The largest fine previously handed out by IMRO was 750,000 pounds to fund management group Invesco in June 1993. Invesco was made to pay costs of 1.59 million pounds, compared with the one million costs agreed on Wednesday by the Deutsche fund arms.
Deutsche would also, he said, have to pay around 220 million pounds to make good losses among the 90,000 private investors who had money in the three funds suspended last September.
Over recent years IMRO has become more open about penalising firms which fail to comply with its rules, a change which regulatory sources say can in large part be attributed to Thorpe.
The 42-year-old New Zealander is believed to be in the running for the job of Britain's top financial regulator.
Sir Andrew Large, chairman of the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) was due to stand down at the end of May, but it was announced on Wednesday that he is to carry on for an extra two months.

His replacement is not expected to be announced until after the result of the national election on May 1 when the incoming government will, along with the Bank of England governor, decide on his successor.

Thorpe has been praised for dealing firmly with companies involved in a scandel over pensions mis-selling. He was drafted in as IMRO's head in July 1993 to secure the frontline regulator's future after the Robert Maxwell affair.

IMRO regulated Bishopsgate Investment Management and London and Bishopsgate Investment Management, two of the companies that looked after the Maxwell pension funds and in which an unexplained shortfall of 440 million pounds was discovered after Maxwell's death.

IMRO, one of three self-regulating organisations, says its mission is "to protect investors by setting and promoting standards of integrity, competition and solvency for those IMRO regulates; and to monitor and enforce those standards effectively and efficiently".
